title: THE BIBLE DOESN’T TEACH “SEX IS DIRTY”—It Teaches That Something Powerful Needs Faithfulness, Boundaries, and Love
paragraphs: THE BIBLE DOESN’T TEACH “SEX IS DIRTY”—It Teaches That Something Powerful Needs Faithfulness, Boundaries, and Love

Maybe the Church never needed to make sex sound disgusting. Maybe we needed to recover something far more beautiful—and far more demanding: God calls it powerful enough to protect, sacred enough for faithfulness, intimate enough for covenant, and precious enough not to be treated casually.
There are people reading this who learned about sex through shame.
Not holiness.
Shame.
Maybe nobody actually said the words, “Sex is dirty.”
They didn’t have to.
You could hear it in the uncomfortable silence.
You could feel it when the subject suddenly changed.
You could see it in the expression on someone’s face whenever desire was mentioned.
And somewhere along the way, some Christians absorbed a strange message that sounded almost biblical:
Good Christians do not really talk about sex.
Good Christians barely desire it.

And if you have struggled sexually, crossed boundaries, watched pornography, slept with someone outside marriage, committed adultery, carried secret fantasies, or simply found yourself wrestling with desires you were ashamed to admit existed...
perhaps you started wondering whether something about your body itself was disgusting to God.
But then you actually open the Bible.
And something surprising happens.
The story does not begin with sex being dirty.
It begins with God creating human beings embodied, male and female, declaring His creation “very good” (Genesis 1:27–31).
Before pornography.
Before adultery.
Before exploitation.
Before lust distorted another human being into an object.
Before sin fractured human intimacy.
There was a man.
There was a woman.
There was covenantal union.
And there was no shame.
Genesis 2:24 reaches back to the foundation:
“Therefore a man shall leave his father and his mother and hold fast to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.”
The Hebrew gives us language worth slowing down for:
וְדָבַק בְּאִשְׁתּוֹ
ve-davaq be-ishto
“And he shall cling to his wife.”
That word דָּבַק — davaq — carries the sense of clinging, holding fast, remaining closely joined.
Then Scripture says:
וְהָיוּ לְבָשָׂר אֶחָד
ve-hayu levasar echad
“And they shall become one flesh.”
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד.
Basar echad.
“One flesh.”
Notice what Scripture does not say.
It does not introduce marital intimacy as a filthy necessity God reluctantly tolerates so humanity can reproduce.
It places “one flesh” inside the creation account itself.
That changes the conversation.
Sexuality is not evil because it is powerful.
Its power is one of the reasons Scripture refuses to treat it casually.
Fire can warm a home.
Fire can also consume one.
The problem is not that fire exists.
The question is whether it is being honored according to its nature.
And perhaps that is where both religious shame and modern sexual culture make opposite mistakes.
One side can make sex seem inherently filthy.
The other can make it seem almost meaningless.
Scripture permits neither.
The Bible does not say your body is disposable.
It says your body matters so much that what you do with it matters.
It does not say sexual union means nothing.
It says sexual union means enough that faithfulness matters.
It does not say desire itself proves you are corrupt.
It teaches that our desires, like every other part of fallen humanity, must come under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
That is why biblical boundaries are not evidence that God hates sexuality.
They are evidence that God refuses to trivialize it.
Listen to the startling language of Hebrews 13:4:
Τίμιος ὁ γάμος ἐν πᾶσιν καὶ ἡ κοίτη ἀμίαντος.
Timios ho gamos en pasin kai hē koitē amiantos.
A close rendering is:
“Let marriage be held in honor among all, and the marriage bed be undefiled.”
Τίμιος — timios.
Precious.
Valued.
Honored.
And then comes ἀμίαντος — amiantos.
Undefiled.
Unstained.
Think about that.
Scripture can speak of the marriage bed and call it undefiled.
The Bible's answer to sexual immorality, therefore, cannot simply be summarized as “sex is dirty.”
The biblical picture is more beautiful than that.
Marriage is to be honored.
The marriage bed is to remain undefiled.
And sexual immorality and adultery are treated seriously before God.
The distinction matters.
Because there is an enormous difference between saying, “This is filthy, so stay away from it,” and saying, “This is precious, so do not desecrate it.”
One produces disgust.
The other can produce reverence.
One can make a wounded person hate himself.
The other calls a sinner to repentance while showing him that God created something worth restoring.
And this is where the Bible becomes uncomfortable for almost everybody.
Because recovering the goodness of sexuality does not mean erasing biblical boundaries.
Actually, it gives us a reason for them.
Paul writes in 1 Corinthians 6:18:
Φεύγετε τὴν πορνείαν.
Pheugete tēn porneian.
“Flee sexual immorality.”
Not negotiate with it.
Not see how close you can stand to it.
Not build your secret life around it while maintaining your Christian appearance.
Flee.
The command is forceful because Paul understands that your body is not spiritually irrelevant.

Only a few verses later, he reminds believers that their bodies belong to Christ, that the body is a temple of the Holy Spirit, that they were bought with a price, and therefore they are to glorify God in their bodies (1 Corinthians 6:19–20).
Do you see what Christianity does here?
It refuses to say your body is worthless.
It says almost the opposite.
Your body matters to God.
Your sexuality matters to God.
Your choices matter to God.
What happens behind a locked bedroom door matters to God.
What happens on a glowing screen at 1:17 in the morning matters to God.
How you look at another human being matters.
How you treat your spouse matters.
What you do with somebody else's vulnerability matters.
Whether your desire becomes service or selfishness matters.
Whether intimacy expresses faithfulness or betrayal matters.
Whether another person's body becomes someone you love sacrificially or something you consume selfishly matters.
Not because God despises the body.
Because He created it.
That means Christian sexual ethics cannot merely be a list of things you are forbidden to do.
At its deepest level, it asks:
What does love require?
What does covenant require?
What does faithfulness require?
What honors Christ?
What protects another person's dignity instead of exploiting it?
What allows me to look at another image-bearer and remember:
You are not a product for my appetite.
You are not pixels for my private consumption.
You are not an experience for me to collect.
You belong first to God.
And so do I.
That truth changes things.
Especially when nobody else is watching.
Maybe this article is hitting somewhere you hoped nobody would touch.
Maybe your browser history tells a different story from your Sunday worship.
Maybe you keep promising God, “This is the last time.”
Then the loneliness comes.
The temptation comes.
The message arrives.
The memory comes back.
The screen lights up.
And suddenly the conviction that felt powerful Sunday morning feels very far away on Tuesday night.
Maybe you have crossed a line you once swore you never would.
Maybe you slept with someone because you desperately wanted to feel loved.
Maybe you gave your body hoping someone would give you their heart.
And they left.
Maybe you are married, but pornography has quietly trained your eyes to compare your spouse with bodies that were never yours to possess.
Maybe your spouse does not know.
Maybe they know, and trust has been shattered.
Maybe you were unfaithful.
Maybe someone was unfaithful to you.
Maybe sex was used against you.
And if someone violated, coerced, exploited, or abused you, hear this distinction clearly:
Another person's sexual sin against you is not your moral stain to carry.
Their wrongdoing does not make you dirty.
Jesus never asks victims to call evil good, pretend wounds do not exist, or accept responsibility for another person's abuse.
Perhaps your story is different.
Maybe you grew up hearing so much fear around sexuality that even within marriage you struggle to receive marital intimacy without feeling ashamed.
The Bible has room to correct that distortion too.

Paul speaks remarkably openly in 1 Corinthians 7 about mutual marital responsibility. Husband and wife are both addressed. Neither spouse is presented merely as an object existing for the gratification of the other. There is mutuality, responsibility, consideration, and belonging.
Biblical marital intimacy is not a license for selfishness.
Marriage never transforms coercion into love.
The pattern Jesus gives His people is sacrificial love.
Christ does not teach us to consume people.
He teaches us to love them.
And this is why Christian sexual holiness is far richer than virginity before a wedding.
A person can technically preserve a physical boundary while cultivating lust, manipulation, pride, objectification, cruelty, or selfishness.
Jesus goes after the heart.
He does not merely ask what your hands have done.
He confronts what your heart has learned to worship.
That is terrifying.
Until you remember who is asking.
Jesus.
The One who sat near people respectable religion preferred to avoid.
The One who knew people's histories without needing gossip to inform Him.
The One who could expose sin without exploiting sinners.
The One who could say, “Go, and from now on sin no more,” while refusing to join the mob hungry for condemnation (John 8:1–11).
Grace did not tell people sin did not matter.
Grace gave sinners somewhere to go with it.
That is the Gospel.
And somebody needs that sentence tonight.
Because perhaps you have confused conviction with hopelessness.
Conviction says:
Come into the light.
Shame says:
Hide because if anybody really knew you, they would leave.
Conviction says:
Confess.
Shame says:
Pretend.
Conviction says:
Repent.
Shame says:
You are permanently defined by what you did.
But Jesus did not go to the cross merely to improve the public behavior of people who were already clean.
Christ died for sinners.
Real ones.
People with histories.
People with secrets.
People who knew exactly what it meant to have something in their past they could not undo.
And Scripture does not romanticize that past.
It does something better.
It announces redemption.
Paul lists patterns of serious sin in 1 Corinthians 6, including sexual sin, and then delivers three of the most hope-filled words a broken person could hear:
“And such were some of you.”
Were.
Not because their histories vanished.
Not because consequences magically disappeared.
Not because sin suddenly became harmless.
But because Jesus Christ had intervened.
Paul continues by speaking of being washed, sanctified, and justified in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ and by the Spirit of God (1 Corinthians 6:11).
That is Christianity.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Grace rewriting what the scandal gets to mean.
You may have sexual sin in your story.
Sexual sin does not have to be the final author of your story.
You may have betrayed someone.
Repent.
You may need to confess.
You may need accountability.
You may need to delete something.
Block someone.
End something.
Tell the truth.
Seek wise pastoral help.
Seek professional help where trauma, compulsion, abuse, or deep relational damage is involved.
You may need to stop calling bondage “just the way I am.”
But repentance is not God standing over you demanding that you crawl back to Him while He enjoys your humiliation.
The Gospel announces that God has acted in Christ to reconcile sinners to Himself.
Jesus bore sin.
Jesus died.
Jesus rose.
Jesus saves.
And because He lives, repentance is not walking toward a grave.
It is turning toward Life.
This is where boundaries begin to look different.
“No” can become an act of love.
Waiting can become worship.
Faithfulness can become freedom.
Self-control can become evidence that desire is no longer your master.
And marriage can become more than permission to have sex.
It becomes covenant.
A place where nakedness was meant to meet faithfulness.
Where vulnerability was meant to meet safety.
Where desire was meant to learn love.
Where bodies are not merchandise.
Where intimacy is not performance.
Where neither husband nor wife is reduced to an instrument.
Where the question slowly changes from “What can I get?” to “How can I love?”
That does not make marriage effortless.
It makes it holy ground for discipleship.
And for the unmarried Christian, Scripture does not treat you as half a human waiting for sexuality to complete you.
Jesus Himself destroys that lie.
The most complete human life ever lived was not completed by sexual experience.
Christ was fully human, fully holy, and unmarried.
So your worth is not measured by whether somebody desires your body.
Your adulthood is not validated by sexual experience.
Your identity is not secured by romantic attention.
And marriage is not your savior.
Jesus is.
That matters in a culture constantly whispering that you are missing something essential unless somebody wants you sexually.
You are not a body desperately waiting for another person to give you value.
You bear God's image.
And if you belong to Christ, you have been purchased at immeasurable cost.
This is why purity cannot simply mean “never having messed up.”
If that were Christianity, enormous numbers of people would have no road home.
Biblical purity ultimately depends on something far greater than an untouched past.
It points us toward the cleansing grace of God and a present life increasingly surrendered to Him.
Maybe you cannot become the person who never sinned sexually.
But through Christ, you can become a person who no longer hides.
You can tell the truth.
You can repent.
You can receive forgiveness.
You can learn faithfulness.
You can rebuild integrity one surrendered decision at a time.
You can become trustworthy again where restoration is possible.
You can stop feeding the secret that has been feeding on you.
And perhaps tonight the bravest prayer you can pray is not impressive at all.
“Jesus, I need You.”
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to publish the details of your private life. But you also do not have to keep pretending that everything is fine.
There should be places in the Body of Christ where those words are not invitations for gossip but invitations for prayer.
If you know a young believer being discipled more aggressively by pornography, hookup culture, social media, or shame than by Scripture, send this to them.
Temptation has a strange way of making us forget what conviction sounded like when our minds were clear.
Come back when you need to remember.

Invite your family, your friends, struggling believers, seekers, lukewarm Christians, and even the person who does not yet believe to follow too. We want this community to remain a place for daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, repentance, grace, and spiritual nourishment centered on Jesus Christ.
It cannot.
Not because giving earns salvation.
It never will.
Your giving before God is a matter that deserves biblical conviction, wisdom, and a willing heart.
Scripture says, “God loves a cheerful giver” (2 Corinthians 9:7). Paul also gratefully recognized believers who financially partnered with Gospel ministry (Philippians 4:15–18).
It is partnership.
It is helping keep Scripture moving through newsfeeds filled with noise.
It is helping put truth in front of the exhausted believer.
Grace in front of the ashamed.
Conviction in front of the comfortable.
The Gospel in front of the person who thought Christianity had nothing left to say to them.
One share can place the message in front of someone we could never have reached ourselves.
One tag can become a conversation.
One comment can make another struggling Christian realize they are not the only person fighting.
One saved article can become a midnight reminder.
And one surrendered life can become evidence that Jesus Christ still transforms sinners.
Because Christianity's message about sex was never:
“Your body is disgusting.”
It is far closer to this:
Your body belongs to God.
People are not objects.
Desire is not your master.
Marriage is honorable.
Faithfulness matters.
Sexual immorality is serious.
Love refuses exploitation.
Holiness requires boundaries.
Repentance is real.
Grace is available.
Forgiveness was purchased at the cross.
And no sexual history is powerful enough to make the blood of Jesus powerless.
So stop calling what God created evil.
And stop calling what God forbids harmless.
We do not need shame without truth.
We do not need desire without boundaries.
We do not need legalism without grace.
And we do not need grace stripped of repentance.
We need Jesus.
Jesus in our marriages.
Jesus in our singleness.
Jesus in our desires.
Jesus in our bedrooms.
Jesus in our browser histories.
Jesus in our wounds.
Jesus in our secrets.
Jesus in our repentance.
Jesus in our restoration.
Jesus at the center of everything.
Perhaps your scandal is real.
But scandal does not get the last word when Jesus Christ becomes the Author of what comes next.
Your worst chapter may explain where you have been—but only Jesus gets to decide what redemption can make of the pages that remain.
